passage:
"Rajni, where's your nose? Nose? Where's your nose, Rajni?" Grandpa asked, fast, leaning close.
Rajni just looked at him.
"She doesn't know," he said.
"Wait," said Bhavna, her mother. "Ask once. Then count to five in your head."
Grandpa sighed. "Rajni, where's your nose?"
Silence. One, two, three, four... Rajni slowly lifted one finger and pressed it to her nose. Then she grinned.

qa.q: What did Bhavna tell Grandpa to do after asking?
qa.a: To ask once and then count to five in his head.

qa.q: What was Rajni doing during the long silence, and how did she feel at the end?
qa.a: She was probably working out the question rather than ignoring him; her grin at the end suggests she felt proud once she answered.

qa.q: Why did waiting work better than repeating the question fast?
qa.a: Waiting gave Rajni time to process the question, while fast repeats gave her no room to answer.

qa.q: How might Grandpa feel when Rajni touches her nose?
qa.a: He would likely feel surprised and pleased, realising she knew all along. 😊

grounding: A mother shows a grandfather that his toddler granddaughter answers after a pause when given time to process.

passage: Playgroup note, Monday. At snack time I held up an apple and a banana and asked Karthik, "Which one?" He looked at both and said nothing. I wanted to ask again, but I waited, counting slowly in my head. After what felt like a long time, he pointed at the banana and said, "Nana." At home, try asking once and then waiting a few seconds; he seems to need that time to answer. Payal, playgroup teacher

qa.q: Which fruit did Karthik choose?
qa.a: The banana, saying "Nana."

qa.q: What was Karthik likely thinking while he looked at both fruits in silence?
qa.a: He was likely thinking and deciding rather than ignoring Payal; he seemed calm and content once he answered.

qa.q: What did Payal suggest the family try at home?
qa.a: Ask once and then wait a few seconds so Karthik has time to answer.

qa.q: How might Payal have felt during the long pause?
qa.a: Payal felt the urge to ask again, perhaps a little impatient, but held back and was rewarded with his answer.

grounding: A teacher waits after asking a toddler a question and finds he answers when given time to process.

passage:
Chaitanya crouched by the village well with his little niece. "Mehak, where's the cow?"
Mehak stared at the ground. Chaitanya opened his mouth to ask again, louder. Then he stopped, and just waited.
A dog barked. A bucket clanked. Mehak slowly turned, lifted her arm toward the shed, and said, "Moo."
"Yes! The cow's in the shed," Chaitanya said, and Mehak's face lit up.

qa.q: Where was the cow?
qa.a: In the shed.

qa.q: What was Mehak thinking about while she stared at the ground?
qa.a: She was likely thinking about the question and finding the answer, not ignoring her uncle; her face lighting up shows she was pleased when he understood.

qa.q: What small choice of Chaitanya's made the difference?
qa.a: He stopped himself from asking again louder and simply waited.

qa.q: What would change if Chaitanya had kept asking louder?
qa.a: Mehak might have been confused or overwhelmed and never got to answer.

grounding: An uncle waits instead of repeating a question, and his toddler niece answers after a delay.

passage:
On the doorstep in Mexico City, Sofia was trying to talk with the neighbour about the water cut. Alejandro tugged her skirt. "Mama! Mama! Perro! Perro!" He talked straight over both of them.
The neighbour frowned. Sofia bent down. "One moment. My turn to talk." She finished her sentence, then turned back. "Now your turn. What did you see?" Alejandro pointed. "Perro!" A small dog was trotting past.

qa.q: What were Sofia and the neighbour talking about?
qa.a: The water cut.

qa.q: What was Alejandro feeling as he talked over them?
qa.a: He was excited about the dog and eager to share it, not trying to be rude; he just didn't know about waiting yet.

qa.q: What did Sofia's "my turn, your turn" teach Alejandro?
qa.a: It showed him a short pause for others and then a clear turn for him, the start of taking turns.

qa.q: How does the neighbour see Alejandro's interrupting?
qa.a: The neighbour seems annoyed and may read it as rudeness, not a toddler's excitement.

grounding: A mother answers her toddler's talking over others with "my turn, your turn" rather than calling it rude.

passage: I'm Seema, Pankaj's big sister. At dinner Papa was telling a story about his office, and Pankaj kept babbling right over him, louder and louder. I thought he was being naughty. Papa stopped and picked up a spoon. "Spoon means your turn, Pankaj." He handed it over. Pankaj babbled into it. Then Papa took it back. "My turn." Pankaj waited, sort of. I don't know if he got it, but it was funny.

qa.q: What did Papa use to show whose turn it was?
qa.a: A spoon.

qa.q: What might Pankaj have been feeling as he babbled over Papa?
qa.a: He probably wanted to join in and be heard, feeling excited rather than naughty; he doesn't yet know how to take turns.

qa.q: What did Papa do that builds the turn-taking habit?
qa.a: He used a simple object and the words "your turn, my turn" to show when to talk and when to wait.

qa.q: How does Seema see Pankaj's babbling?
qa.a: Seema first thinks he is being naughty, then finds Papa's spoon game funny, though unsure if it worked.

grounding: A sister sees her father teach her toddler brother turn-taking with "your turn, my turn" instead of scolding.

passage:
Monday: Ujjwal was on a work call at home. Rukmini stood by his knee, shouting "Pa! Pa! Pa!" over every sentence.
Wednesday: at breakfast Ujjwal paused mid-sentence and said, "Your turn." Rukmini babbled a long string. "My turn," he said, and she listened for a moment.
The next Monday: Rukmini babbled, then stopped on her own and looked at him, waiting for his reply.

qa.q: What was Ujjwal doing on Monday?
qa.a: He was on a work call at home.

qa.q: What was Rukmini feeling when she shouted over the call?
qa.a: She wanted her father's attention and felt left out, not being rude; she simply didn't know how to wait yet.

qa.q: What habit helped Rukmini begin to take turns?
qa.a: Ujjwal pausing and saying "Your turn" and "My turn", which showed her the pattern.

qa.q: How might Ujjwal feel the next Monday when Rukmini waits?
qa.a: He would likely feel pleased and touched that she is learning to leave space for him. 🙂

grounding: Over a week a father models brief pauses and "your turn, my turn", and his toddler begins to wait.

passage:
The power had gone out in the village, and the night was hot and still. Madhuri tossed and whimpered on the charpai.
Preeti lay beside her, fanning her with a folded newspaper, and began to sing an old lullaby, slow and low. She sang off key; she always did.
Madhuri's whimpers slowed. Her hand found Preeti's arm and stayed there. By the third verse, her breathing was deep and even.

qa.q: What did Preeti fan Madhuri with?
qa.a: A folded newspaper.

qa.q: Why did Madhuri settle even though Preeti sang off key?
qa.a: She felt safe with her mother close, and the slow, warm rhythm mattered more than the tune; her hand on Preeti's arm shows she felt comforted.

qa.q: What would you tell a parent who thinks they can't sing well enough?
qa.a: That a slow, warm voice and closeness soothe a child far more than a perfect tune.

qa.q: What was the hot night like for Preeti?
qa.a: It was probably tiring and uncomfortable, yet she stayed close and kept singing for Madhuri.

grounding: A toddler settles to her mother's off-key lullaby, soothed by the rhythm, warmth and closeness rather than the tune.

passage:
In the Sydney flat, Xin, Jamal's babysitter, played a lullaby from the speaker and laid him in the cot. Jamal kept crying.
She turned the speaker off, lifted him onto her shoulder and walked slowly up and down, humming the same tune under her breath, very slow.
Jamal's crying faded into small hiccups. His head grew heavy on her shoulder.

qa.q: Where did Xin first lay Jamal?
qa.a: In the cot.

qa.q: Why might Jamal have settled to Xin's humming but not the speaker?
qa.a: He likely felt safer with her warmth and slow walking rhythm; the same tune alone didn't comfort him, but with her closeness he felt calm.

qa.q: What could Xin try at the next bedtime?
qa.a: Start with holding and humming slowly, then lay him down once he is calm.

qa.q: How might Xin feel as Jamal's head grows heavy?
qa.a: She would likely feel relieved and warm, knowing her closeness settled him.

grounding: A toddler settles to his carer's slow humming and closeness, not to the same lullaby played from a speaker.

passage: My name is Kavitha, and I was on the night bus to Siliguri. Across the aisle, a grandmother held a little girl called Pema, who was crying hard. The grandmother began to hum something slow in a language I didn't know, rocking gently with the bus. I couldn't understand a word. But I watched Pema's fists open and her crying fade. Maybe it was the song. Maybe it was just being held like that.

qa.q: Where was the bus going?
qa.a: To Siliguri.

qa.q: What might Pema have been feeling as her fists opened?
qa.a: She was likely beginning to feel safe and calm in her grandmother's arms, soothed by the slow humming and rocking.

qa.q: What does the grandmother's approach show about soothing small children?
qa.a: That a slow rhythm, a warm voice and being held can calm a child, whatever the words or tune.

qa.q: How might the grandmother feel as Pema settles?
qa.a: She would probably feel relieved and tender after the hard crying.

grounding: A passenger sees a toddler settle to her grandmother's slow humming, the calm coming from closeness and rhythm.

passage:
In their Bengaluru flat, Gopika sat on the floor stacking cups, humming to herself, "Mmm-mm-mmm, mmm-mm-mmm," over and over.
Naveen, working at the table, hummed the same little tune back.
Gopika stopped. She looked round at him, smiled, and hummed it again, a little louder. He hummed back. They went on like that until the tower fell.

qa.q: What was Gopika stacking?
qa.a: Cups.

qa.q: What was Gopika feeling as she hummed to herself?
qa.a: She was content and relaxed, absorbed in her play; her smile at Naveen shows she was delighted when he joined in.

qa.q: What did Naveen do that builds connection?
qa.a: He echoed her tune back, turning her private humming into a little musical conversation.

qa.q: How might Naveen feel humming back while working?
qa.a: He probably enjoys the small shared moment, finding it a pleasant break.

grounding: A toddler hums a wordless tune while playing, and her father echoes it back, building connection.

passage:
"Listen," said Payal. "She's singing."
From the bath came, "Oo-ah-oo, oo-ah-oo."
"What song is that?" asked Uma's father.
"Her own." Payal leaned over the tub and sang it back, "Oo-ah-oo."
Uma splashed and laughed. "Oo-ah-OO!"
"Now she's changed it."
"Oo-ah-OO!" Payal sang. Uma clapped the water.

qa.q: Where was Uma singing?
qa.a: In the bath.

qa.q: What does Uma's cooing and laughing show about her feelings?
qa.a: She was content and happy in the bath, and delighted when Payal sang her tune back.

qa.q: Why does echoing Uma's tune help her?
qa.a: It builds connection and lets her play with sound and rhythm, the start of language.

qa.q: How does Uma's father react at first?
qa.a: He's curious and asks what song it is, not realising it's her own made-up tune.

grounding: A toddler coos a wordless melody in the bath, and her mother echoes it back.

passage: Childminder's note, Friday. Kunal hummed a little tune the whole time he was painting today, getting louder when he mixed the blue and yellow. When he bumped his elbow later, he sat quietly and hummed the same tune, softer, rubbing his arm. I hummed it with him and he leaned on me. His humming seems to be both how he enjoys himself and how he calms down. Vasudha, childminder

qa.q: What colours did Kunal mix?
qa.a: Blue and yellow.

qa.q: What was Kunal feeling when he hummed after bumping his elbow?
qa.a: He was hurt and a bit upset, and the soft humming helped him soothe himself; earlier, the louder humming showed contentment.

qa.q: What did Vasudha do when he hummed after the bump?
qa.a: Vasudha hummed the tune with him, which let him lean in for comfort.

qa.q: How might Kunal's family feel reading the note?
qa.a: They would likely feel glad to understand his humming better and reassured he was comforted.

grounding: A childminder notes a toddler hums with contentment while painting and to soothe himself after a bump, and echoes the tune.

passage:
For weeks, Shankar had slipped out of the Chennai daycare while Jaya was busy, and every day she searched the room, sobbing. This week he tried something new: two hugs, one high-five, and a wave at the window.
Today Jaya clung to his neck and cried. Then she took the high-five. Then she cried again. But she went to the window and waved, tears on her cheeks, and turned back to the blocks.

qa.q: What was the new goodbye Shankar tried?
qa.a: Two hugs, one high-five and a wave at the window.

qa.q: What was Jaya feeling at drop-off today?
qa.a: She was sad about the goodbye, clinging and crying, but also able to wave and turn to the blocks, showing mixed feelings she could manage.

qa.q: Why does the ritual work better than slipping out?
qa.a: Because Jaya knows what will happen and when he leaves, so she doesn't have to search the room in fear.

qa.q: How might Shankar feel walking away after the wave?
qa.a: He probably feels a pang at her tears, but also relief that she turned back to play.

grounding: A father replaces sneaking away with a short goodbye ritual, which helps his toddler manage mixed feelings at drop-off.

passage:
"Just slip out while he's playing, Imran," said Ujjwal's mother. "He won't notice."
"Last time he noticed. He searched every room and screamed for an hour."
"So what, then?"
"Our goodbye." Imran knelt. "Ujjwal. Bye-bye kiss. Papa comes after nap."
Ujjwal's lip wobbled. He cried and held on. Imran kissed him, said it once more and stood. Ujjwal cried, then lifted a hand and waved.

qa.q: When did Imran say he would come back?
qa.a: After nap.

qa.q: What was Ujjwal feeling at the goodbye?
qa.a: He was sad and upset, crying and holding on, but able to wave, showing mixed feelings that the ritual helped him manage.

qa.q: Why did Imran choose the goodbye over slipping out?
qa.a: Because slipping out last time left Ujjwal searching and screaming, while a clear, short goodbye tells him what is happening.

qa.q: How does Ujjwal's mother see the goodbye at first?
qa.a: She thinks slipping out would be easier and that he wouldn't notice.

grounding: A father uses a short, predictable goodbye rather than sneaking away, helping his toddler cope with a sad drop-off.

passage: Daycare note, Thursday. Until last week, Kishore's mother left while he was distracted, and he would cry at the door for a long time. This week we agreed on a ritual: one song, one hug, and a wave from the window. Today he cried during the song, hugged her tight, and then ran to the window to wave. He sniffed for a few minutes and then joined the sand tray. Much quicker than before. Preeti, daycare teacher

qa.q: What did Kishore join after sniffing?
qa.a: The sand tray.

qa.q: What was Kishore feeling during the new goodbye?
qa.a: He was still sad, crying during the song and hugging tight, but the familiar steps helped him feel safe enough to wave and settle quickly.

qa.q: What would you advise other parents at this daycare?
qa.a: Use a short, predictable goodbye ritual instead of leaving while the child is distracted.

qa.q: How might Kishore's mother feel reading the note?
qa.a: She would likely feel relieved and encouraged that he settled much quicker.

grounding: A teacher records how a short, predictable goodbye ritual helped a toddler settle faster than sneaking away.

passage: Daycare note, Tuesday. At pick-up time Himani waves "bah-bah!" to everyone, the cook, the guard, the other parents. But today, when the visiting inspector bent down and said hello, she hid behind my legs and wouldn't look. Her mother said, "Say hello, Himani!" I suggested we let her be. When the inspector was leaving, Himani peeked out and waved a tiny wave. Salma, daycare teacher

qa.q: Whom does Himani usually wave to at pick-up?
qa.a: The cook, the guard and the other parents.

qa.q: What was Himani feeling when she hid from the inspector?
qa.a: She was shy with a new person; her tiny wave later shows she was still interested once she had time.

qa.q: Which choice of Salma's worked, and why?
qa.a: Suggesting they let her be worked, because without pressure Himani found her own moment to wave.

qa.q: How does Himani's mother see the hiding?
qa.a: She seems to want Himani to be polite, perhaps feeling a little embarrassed in front of the inspector.

grounding: A teacher sees a toddler wave to familiar people and hide from a new one, and does not force a greeting.

passage:
At the small-town bus stand, Aadhya waved her whole arm at the conductor hanging out of the bus door. "Hai! Hai!" He waved back, and she squealed.
Then the temple priest stopped and bent down. "And hello to you, little one!" Aadhya pressed her face into her Bua's sari.
"Say namaste," someone said.
Himani, her Bua, shook her head. "She'll say it another day." The priest smiled and walked on.

qa.q: Who was hanging out of the bus door?
qa.a: The conductor.

qa.q: What was Aadhya feeling when she pressed her face into her Bua's sari?
qa.a: She felt shy with the priest bending close, even though she had been happily waving at the conductor from a distance.

qa.q: Which of Himani's choices respected Aadhya, and why?
qa.a: Not forcing her to say namaste respected her shyness and let her greet when she felt ready.

qa.q: How might the priest see Aadhya hiding?
qa.a: The priest seems understanding, smiling and walking on without taking offence.

grounding: A toddler waves and babbles hello to a familiar face but hides from a stranger, and her aunt doesn't force a greeting.

passage:
Every morning in Sapporo, Hiroshi stood at the window and waved "bai-bai!" to the garbage truck crew. They always waved back.
On Saturday, a new neighbour at the gate smiled and said, "Good morning, Hiroshi!" He ducked behind Hana's coat.
Hana didn't pull him forward. She smiled at the neighbour. "He's shy with new faces." From behind the coat, Hiroshi peeped out and watched.

qa.q: Whom does Hiroshi wave to every morning?
qa.a: The garbage truck crew.

qa.q: What was Hiroshi feeling when he ducked behind Hana's coat?
qa.a: He felt shy and unsure with a new face, even though he's friendly with people he knows.

qa.q: What did Hana do that respected Hiroshi?
qa.a: She didn't pull him forward, and explained his shyness kindly to the neighbour.

qa.q: How might the new neighbour feel when Hiroshi hides?
qa.a: The neighbour might feel a little disappointed, but Hana's words help them understand it isn't personal.

grounding: A toddler waves to familiar faces and hides from a new neighbour, and his mother doesn't force a greeting.

passage:
Amara had been away for four nights for work. When she opened the door of the flat in Nairobi, Mei, on the rug, froze for a second. Then her whole face lit up. She squealed, dropped her toy and toddled at top speed across the room, arms out, nearly falling into Amara's legs.
Amara scooped her up. "I'm back, like I said." Mei patted her cheeks with both hands.

qa.q: How many nights had Amara been away?
qa.a: Four nights.

qa.q: What was Mei feeling when her face lit up?
qa.a: She felt pure joy and relief at her mother's return, rushing to her with her arms out.

qa.q: What could help Mei with Amara's future trips?
qa.a: Keeping clear goodbyes and returning when promised, as Amara reminded her, so Mei learns to trust the pattern.

qa.q: What is it like for Amara to be greeted this way?
qa.a: She likely feels overjoyed and relieved to be home. 🤍

grounding: A toddler lights up and toddles to her returning mother, showing joy and secure attachment.

passage: I'm Ishita, and I live across the lane from Usha's family. Every evening at six, her grandmother comes back from the temple with a bag of flowers. And every evening, the moment the gate creaks, little Usha lights up. She drops whatever she's holding and toddles to the gate as fast as her legs will go, reaching up. It's the same every day. Maybe she knows the sound of the gate. Maybe she just knows it's time.

qa.q: What does Usha's grandmother bring back from the temple?
qa.a: A bag of flowers.

qa.q: What might Usha be feeling when the gate creaks?
qa.a: She is likely excited and joyful, expecting her grandmother; lighting up and reaching shows a strong, trusting bond.

qa.q: What keeps Usha's welcome so steady?
qa.a: The grandmother coming back at the same time every day, which makes the reunion predictable.

qa.q: How might Usha's grandmother feel coming through the gate?
qa.a: She probably feels loved and happy to be greeted so eagerly.

grounding: A neighbour sees a toddler light up and toddle to her returning grandmother every evening, a sign of secure attachment.

passage:
Monday: Kishore started an early shift and left before Anirban woke. When he came home, Anirban turned away and fussed.
Thursday: Kishore woke him gently first. "Papa going to work. Back after lunch." Anirban frowned but waved. When the door opened after lunch, he lit up and reached.
The next Tuesday: at the sound of the key, Anirban was already toddling to the door, squealing.

qa.q: When did Kishore start leaving before Anirban woke?
qa.a: On Monday, when he started an early shift.

qa.q: Why did Anirban turn away on Monday?
qa.a: He was likely upset and confused that his father had gone without a goodbye.

qa.q: What change helped Anirban welcome his father again?
qa.a: A clear, predictable goodbye with a promise of when he'd be back, which Kishore then kept.

qa.q: How might Kishore feel when Anirban toddles to the door?
qa.a: He would likely feel relieved and happy that the goodbye routine rebuilt Anirban's joy.

grounding: Over a week a predictable goodbye helps a toddler move from turning away to eagerly welcoming his returning father.

passage: I'm Thomas. I live on the floor above Nikita's family. On Saturday, on the stairs, Nikita stopped and pointed down at the landing. "Ca! Ca!" A white cat was curled there. Her mother said, "Cat! A white cat." Nikita said, "Ca," again, very pleased, then pointed at my shoes. "Shoo!" Her mother laughed. "Yes, shoes!" I don't know how many words she knows. She seemed to want us all to look.

qa.q: What was curled on the landing?
qa.a: A white cat.

qa.q: What might Nikita be feeling as she pointed and named things?
qa.a: She seemed pleased and excited to share what she noticed, wanting everyone to look.

qa.q: What did Nikita's mother do that helps Nikita's vocabulary?
qa.a: She named back what Nikita pointed at, "Cat! A white cat" and "shoes", adding words.

qa.q: How does Thomas experience the moment?
qa.a: Thomas seems amused and charmed at being included when she points at the shoes.

grounding: A neighbour sees a toddler point and name things to share interest, and her mother names them back.

passage:
Sunday night: Amandeep pointed out of the window. "Oon!" Urmila, his grandmother, said, "Moon! Big round moon."
Wednesday: on the road, he pointed and shouted, "Ta!" as a tractor went by. "Tractor!" said Urmila. "Red tractor."
The next Sunday: Amandeep took Urmila's hand, pulled her to the window, pointed up and said, "Moon!"

qa.q: What went by on the road on Wednesday?
qa.a: A red tractor.

qa.q: What was Amandeep feeling when he pulled Urmila to the window?
qa.a: He was excited and proud to share the moon with her, wanting her to look with him.

qa.q: What habit of Urmila's helped Amandeep?

qa.q: How might Urmila feel when Amandeep says "Moon!" himself?
qa.a: She would likely feel proud and delighted, seeing the word he learned from her. 🙂

grounding: Over a week a toddler points and names things, and his grandmother names back until he uses the full word.

passage:
At the fruit market in Mumbai, Chandrika was bargaining over mangoes. Sonali, on her hip, pointed at a pile of bananas. "Nana! Nana!"
Chandrika kept talking. Sonali tugged her collar. "Nana!"
Chandrika stopped, turned and looked. "Banana! Yellow bananas." Sonali beamed and pointed at the next pile. "Mmm?" "Mangoes," said Chandrika, and the fruit seller laughed.

qa.q: What was Chandrika bargaining over?
qa.a: Mangoes.

qa.q: Why did Sonali tug Chandrika's collar?
qa.a: She wanted her mother to notice and share what she'd found, feeling ignored while Chandrika bargained.

qa.q: What changed when Chandrika stopped to name the bananas?
qa.a: Sonali felt heard and kept sharing, and got new words for each fruit.

qa.q: How might the fruit seller see the moment?
qa.a: The seller seems amused, enjoying Sonali naming the fruit.

grounding: A mother stops to name back what her toddler points at, and the child keeps sharing.

passage:
Monday: Amandeep pointed at the kettle in Hafsa's kitchen. "Wha-dat?" Hafsa gave a long explanation about boiling water. He wandered off.
Wednesday: "Wha-dat?" at the kettle again. Hafsa smiled. "Kettle." Amandeep beamed.
The next Monday: he pointed at the kettle, looked at Hafsa and asked, "Wha-dat?" with a grin. He knew. She smiled back. "Kettle, again!" He giggled.

qa.q: What did Amandeep point at in Hafsa's kitchen?
qa.a: The kettle.

qa.q: Why did Amandeep keep asking "Wha-dat?" when he already knew?
qa.a: He wanted Hafsa's attention and the shared smile more than the answer, and he felt happy when she played along.

qa.q: What did Hafsa learn about answering?
qa.a: That a short name and a smile work better than a long explanation, since the question is often social.

qa.q: How might Hafsa feel when Amandeep asks again with a grin?
qa.a: She likely feels amused and fond, recognising the question as a game between them.

grounding: Over a week an adult learns that a toddler's "what-that?" is a social question best answered with a name and a smile.

passage:
On the Delhi metro, Suraj pointed at everything. "Dat? Dat?" His voice rose at the end every time. The door. The map. A lady's red bag.
"Door. Map. Bag," said Swati, his mother, with a smile each time.
A man across the aisle sighed loudly. Swati kept going, short and smiling. Suraj pointed at the man's hat. "Dat?"
"Hat," said the man, and he smiled a little too.

qa.q: What did Suraj point at on the man?
qa.a: His hat.

qa.q: What did Suraj want when he asked "Dat?" with a rising voice?
qa.a: He was curious and wanted his mother's attention and a name for each thing; he felt happy to be answered.

qa.q: Which of Swati's choices worked, and why?
qa.a: Giving short answers with a smile worked, because it met his curiosity without tiring her or others.

qa.q: How does the man across the aisle change?
qa.a: He starts off annoyed, sighing loudly, but ends up answering "Hat" and smiling a little.

grounding: A mother answers her toddler's rising "Dat?" with short names and smiles, since the question is social as well as curious.

passage:
"Wassat?" Irfan pointed at the wall.
"A clock," said Madhav, the neighbour, looking up from his tea.
"Wassat?"
"Still a clock."
"Wassat?" Irfan giggled.
"He knows it's a clock," said Irfan's mother. "He just likes you answering."
Madhav laughed and leaned down. "A clock. Tick-tock." Irfan shrieked with joy and pointed again.

qa.q: What was Irfan pointing at?
qa.a: A clock on the wall.

qa.q: What did Irfan want when he kept asking "Wassat?"
qa.a: He wanted Madhav's attention and the fun of the game; his giggling shows he was delighted.

qa.q: What could Madhav do if he wants to keep the game fun?
qa.a: Answer briefly with a smile or a sound, like "Tick-tock", as Irfan's mother suggested.

qa.q: How does Irfan's mother see the repeated questions?

passage: I'm Arnab. I deliver milk in the colony, and little Parveen waits for me every morning at her gate. When she sees my bicycle, she squeals, bounces and reaches for the bell. Last week I was ill, and another man took my round. Her mother told me Parveen stood at the gate and just stared at him, very still, then turned and walked back inside. When I came back on Monday, she squealed again.

qa.q: What does Parveen reach for when she sees Arnab?
qa.a: The bell on the bicycle.

qa.q: What might Parveen have been feeling when the other man came?
qa.a: She was probably confused and wary with a stranger in Arnab's place, staring and turning away; her squeal on Monday shows joy at seeing Arnab again.

qa.q: What could the new delivery man do if he has to cover the round again?
qa.a: Keep a friendly distance and let Parveen watch him, without expecting her to greet him.

qa.q: How might Arnab feel being greeted with a squeal?
qa.a: Arnab likely feels pleased and touched to be recognised and missed.

grounding: A milk deliverer notices a toddler greet him with delight and stare and turn away from a stranger in his place.

passage:
Nani arrived from Kolkata on Saturday. Tarun stared at her from Ammi's lap and turned his face away when she smiled.
Tuesday: he sat on the kitchen floor and watched Rehana Nani roll rotis, very serious.
The next Saturday: Rehana came in from the market. Tarun squealed, bounced on his toes and reached up both arms. "Na-na!"

qa.q: Where did Nani arrive from?
qa.a: From Kolkata.

qa.q: What was Tarun feeling when he turned his face away on Saturday?
qa.a: He didn't yet recognise her and felt wary of a new face.

qa.q: What helped Tarun come to know his Nani?
qa.a: Time, and being able to watch her do everyday things like rolling rotis without pressure.

qa.q: How might Rehana feel the next Saturday?
qa.a: She would likely feel delighted and moved that Tarun now recognised and welcomed her. 🤍

grounding: Over a week a toddler moves from staring and turning away from his grandmother to recognising her with delight.

passage:
Maria had been away in Kuwait for eight months. When she walked into the Panaji flat, Elizabeth stared at her from her mother's arms. Then Maria said, "Hello, my Lizzie," in her old sing-song. Elizabeth's face burst into a smile, and she lunged toward her, arms out.
Behind Maria came her new husband. Elizabeth took one look at him and stared, still, then turned her face into Maria's neck.

qa.q: How long had Maria been away?
qa.a: Eight months.

qa.q: What made Elizabeth recognise Maria?
qa.a: Hearing Maria's old sing-song voice; Elizabeth felt joyful and lunged toward her, arms out.

qa.q: What could Maria's husband do to help Elizabeth get to know him?
qa.a: Give her time and keep a gentle distance, letting her watch him until she feels ready.

qa.q: How might Maria's husband feel when Elizabeth turns away?
qa.a: He might feel a little left out, but understand that he is still a stranger to her.

grounding: A toddler recognises a returning family member's voice with delight and stares and turns away from a new person.
